new.pl: Line between secs. 8 and 9, 550 ft south of the quarter post, T137N R27W, Crow Wing County (charter call)
new.v: Spikes, tie plates, coupler pins, camp trash
new.st: The Northern Mississippi Railway was chartered to run "from a point on the line between Section 8 and 9, Township 137, Range 27 in Crow Wing County, 550 feet south of the quarter post" north 28 miles to sec. 27 T141N R28W in Cass County, with a log landing at Cross Lake. The last train ran in 1908 and the rails were sold in 1911. This pin is the south end from the charter's land call.
new.t: Look on LiDAR for the grade running north from here. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 58-59
pinev: Charter land call, chained from the BLM PLSS sec. 8 east line (about 100 m).

new.n: Swan River junction depot grounds (DMR&N and Duluth & Winnipeg)
new.v: Coins, tokens, railroad buttons, lantern parts
new.st: Swan River was the junction of the Duluth, Mississippi River & Northern logging road and the Duluth & Winnipeg, a "busy transfer point during the 1890's for passengers bound for the logging camps". It was also the south end of the Hill City Railway. The Swan River to Kelly Lake track was pulled in 1960.
new.t: Look at the old depot grounds by the crossing. Private land or railroad land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 45-46
pinev: Placed at the GNIS point for Swan River; the depot grounds were at the crossing nearby (about 300 m).

new.n: Mississippi Landing rollway at the Swan River mouth (DMR&N)
new.pl: Mouth of the Swan River on the Mississippi, Itasca County
new.v: Chain, log dogs, spikes, camp trash
new.st: Mississippi Landing was the Duluth, Mississippi River & Northern log rollway "at the mouth of the Swan River on the Mississippi". In 1895 a rollway of "45,000,000 feet" of logs stretched "a mile down the stream". The track from Swan River to the landing was pulled about 1935.
new.t: Look at the river bank below the Swan River mouth on LiDAR for the rollway and the end of the grade. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 42-46
pinev: Swan River mouth from NHDPlus flowlines; the rollway ran up to a mile downstream (about 800 m).

new.n: Armour's National Woodenware plant, Hill City
new.pl: Hill City on Hill Lake, Aitkin County
new.v: Tokens, plant hardware, bottles, rail spikes
new.st: Armour's National Woodenware plant at Hill City was served by the 17.5-mile Hill City Railway (later the Mississippi, Hill City & Western), which ran from 1915 until it was "abandoned 1935". The grade ran northeast toward Swan River.
new.t: Look for the plant site on Hill Lake and the grade northeast on LiDAR. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), p 46 and route map p 202
pinev: Placed at the GNIS point for Hill City; the plant site on Hill Lake is not yet fixed (about 800 m).

new.n: White Oak Lake landing, Minneapolis & Rainy River logging railroad
new.pl: White Oak Lake by Deer River, Itasca County
new.v: Chain, log dogs, spikes, camp trash
new.st: The Minneapolis & Rainy River logging railroad ran "from the landing at White Oak Lake on the Mississippi to Big Fork, 31.69 miles", with branches to Marcell, Bass Lake and Whitefish. In 1918 trains ran to Alder, Craig and Stanley. The rails were pulled in 1932. This is at the edge of the four-hour range.
new.t: Look on the lake shore by Deer River for the landing and the end of the grade. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 36-41
pinev: Placed at the GNIS point for White Oak Lake; the landing on the shore is not yet fixed (about 1.5 km).

new.n: Mitchell & McClure logging railroad junction at Adolph
new.st: The Mitchell & McClure logging railroad ran 12 miles northeast from Adolph and was abandoned in 1900. In 1901 the Minneapolis & North Western reused the grade. Its branches ran to a hoist on Alden Lake (3.5 miles), to Gallagher Lake (1 mile), and from Sucker River to sec. 13 T52N R13W (5.1 miles), with Camp 17 (Colbrath) and Gipson siding. The 19.6 miles east of Alden Junction were abandoned in 1911.
new.t: Look on LiDAR for the grade running northeast from Adolph and for the Alden Lake hoist. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 78, 83-84
pinev: Placed at the GNIS point for Adolph Station (about 300 m).

new.n: Crescent Springs Railroad, Shell Lake Lumber Co. (1881-1901)
new.st: The Crescent Springs Railroad of the Shell Lake Lumber Co. ran from 1881 to about 1901, 84 miles in all. King calls it "Wisconsin's first logging railroad"; Brody gives that title to the 1875-76 Potato Lake line.
new.t: Look for the mill site on the Shell Lake shore and the grades north and east of town on LiDAR. Private land: ask first.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), p 16
pinev: Placed at Shell Lake village; the mill and the grades are not yet fixed (about 1.5 km).

rv12-mn-nickerson.st: King (1981, pp 79-82): Nickerson was a Scanlon-Gipson sawmill town from 1894 to about 1902, with "buildings ... strung out along both sides of the Eastern Minnesota Railway". Its Minneapolis & North Western logging line ran 6 miles east toward the Wisconsin line and 5 miles west to Lake Graham (1897), and was abandoned after the Scanlon mill opened. An 1895 ad names a second mill near Kerrick, with yards at Kerrick, Anoka and Barnum.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 79-82

fr-scanlon-sawmill-village.st: King (1981, p 82): the Scanlon-Gipson sawmill ran from 1901 to 1909; "by 1902 Scanlon had become a thriving community of some 1,200 inhabitants", and the "town of Scanlon proper was situated on top of the hill overlooking the mill", so the mill site is below the hill on the St. Louis River.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), p 82

fr-gull-river-sawmill-station-vanished.st: King (1981, p 48): the Gull River sawmill stood "at the NP crossing of Gull River, about ten miles west of Brainerd" and ran from 1880 to 1893. Its narrow gauge ran 12 miles northwest to Gilpatrick Lake, with a 673-ft trestle over the Gull Lake narrows (1892).
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), pp 48-52

tg-first-logging-rr.st: King (1981, p 16): the Chippewa River & Menomonie Railway ran 6 miles from Potato Lake to "a landing at the Big Bend of the Chippewa", built 1882-83 (Brody says 1875-76). King gives the "first logging railroad" title to the Crescent Springs road at Shell Lake.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), p 16

pfaff-big-bend-landing.st: King (1981, p 16): the Potato Lake logging railroad ended here on a dump trestle, abandoned by the early 1890s.
src: Frank A. King, Minnesota Logging Railroads (1981), p 16
